• Origin: Asia
  • Growth rate: Slow
  • Height: 5 - 10+ cm
  • Light demand: Medium
  • CO2 demand: Low

• Other names: Dwarf water trumpet
  • Difficulty: easy to medium
  • Lighting: medium to high
  • Optimal pH: 5.5 – 7.5
  • Optimal GH: 1 – 20
  • Optimal temperature: 20 – 28 °C (68 – 82 °F)
  • Substrate: needed
  • Growth form: stem
  • Growth rate: very slow
  • Placement: foreground (carpeting)
  • Height: 3 – 8 cm (~1 – 3 inches)
  • Fertilizers: not needed to low
  • CO2: not needed to low
  • Propagation: runners or lateral shoots

Cryptocoryne is a genus of aquatic plants in the family Araceae, which also includes popular aquarium plants such as Anubias and Pistia. The genus is naturally distributed in tropical regions of India, Southeast Asia and New Guinea.

Cryptocoryne parva is native to the central highlands of Sri Lanka near Kandy, where it forms dense colonies along riversides.
Cryptocoryne parva is a small plant suited to a variety of tank sizes, from nano tanks to large tanks. The minimum tank size for this species is 5 gallons (about 19 litres).

Individual plants should be planted a few centimetres apart, and after about six months they will form a cohesive low group of plants. Known for its slow growth, but Nutrition Capsules in the bottom layer will enhance the development.

Planting

Cryptocoryne parva needs a fertile, nutrient-rich substrate and adequate fertilizer. Plant specimens at least 5 cm (2 inches) apart; they spread sideways and after some months form dense carpets. If a large area is to be covered, it is better to start with as many plants as possible.

Use tweezers to push the plant into the substrate, without planting too deeply, to prevent rot or damage.

Newly bought Cryptocoryne often melt after planting, because they are usually grown emersed at the nursery and those leaves die off anyway. Cutting them down lets the plant save energy for adapting and new growth. However, this should not be done with Cryptocoryne parva before planting: it often does not melt, and it does not like being trimmed.

If all the leaves melt away, do not panic. Mark the exact location and wait (sometimes weeks); the plant is probably still alive and new leaves will sprout.

It has a strong, long, branching root system, so the substrate should be at least 6 cm (~2.5 inches) deep. It propagates by lateral shoots directly on the rhizome and by runners. The plant does not necessarily form dense bushes around the mother plant: because of the long runners, it can propagate up to 20 cm (8 inches) away.

Care

The slow growth makes maintenance easier, since regular trimming is unnecessary. Trimming is only needed after some months, once the plants are fully established and form a lush carpet.

Remove dead leaves and keep water values stable to prevent stress and melting. The plant benefits from iron and potassium supplementation; dose the water column with the right amounts. CO2 can be supplied but is not really necessary.

Its slow growth makes it susceptible to green spot algae. If the tank allows, algae-eating species such as Amano shrimp, Nerite snails and Otocinclus catfish will help.

Problems

  • Losing leaves: crypt melt (Cryptocoryne disease) is when the plant sheds all its leaves while adapting to new water conditions; new leaves emerge after some time. It is more frequent in new aquariums because of sudden changes in chemical values, temperature and lighting, and because the plants were raised emersed. Crypts can also be sensitive to high nitrate.
  • Yellowish leaves: pale, yellowish leaves and holes in the leaves are a sign of iron deficiency; dose iron and potassium adequately.
  • Relocation: moving an old plant can be a real problem, since despite its small size it forms massive roots that can uproot a large part of the tank.
  • Slow growth: it grows, but very slowly.
  • Algae: algae are caused by high levels of organic waste and ammonia. Because of slow growth and root feeding, Cryptocoryne parva cannot compete with algae for nutrients in the water column. Its heavy root system can be used here: root tabs are less likely than liquid fertilizer to cause an algae bloom. Do regular water changes, quarantine or disinfect new plants thoroughly, and introduce algae-eating species.

Temperature: the plant thrives in a wide range of temperatures, but the optimum is 20 – 28 °C (68 – 82 °F).

pH: 5.5 – 7.5.

Hardness: optimal GH is 1 – 20 dGH. It is very adaptable and can grow in soft to hard water.

Lighting: unlike most crypts, Cryptocoryne parva is quite demanding about light. It needs medium to high illumination for optimal growth. Do not place it close to tall plants, which could deprive it of enough light.

Substrate: the plant is unlikely to do well in gravel- or sand-only substrate; in that case a lot of root tabs are needed. It thrives best in an enriched substrate, for example ADA Amazonia aqua soil, CaribSea Eco-Complete or Seachem Flourite Black Sand.

CO2: not required. CO2 injection has very little effect on its growth.

Fertilization: the plant appreciates fertilizer; a liquid fertilizer such as Easy Green is fine. Fertilizers rich in iron and potassium help keep the plant healthy and prevent chlorosis (yellowing of leaves from lack of chlorophyll) and holes in the leaves.

If shrimp are kept in the tank, note that high CO2 levels and copper (contained in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Cryptocoryne parva is compatible with most freshwater fish and other aquatic animals that do not eat it.

  • Fish: Zebra danio, barbs, most tetras, discus, angelfish, Corydoras, guppy, molly, swordtail, Otocinclus catfish, etc.
  • Shrimp: all Neocaridina (Red Cherry, Blue Velvet, Black Rose, Snowball, Orange Sakura, Green Jade, Rili, etc.), Caridina species (Crystal Red, Caridina cf. babaulti, Blue Tiger, etc.), Amano, ghost, bamboo and vampire shrimp.
  • Snails: Ramshorn, Nerite, Malaysian trumpet, Japanese trapdoor and mystery snails. Be careful with snails that may harm or devour the plant.

Avoid hostile, aggressive fish that tear up plants, such as Oscars and cichlids like Frontosa, Texas cichlids, Red Devil and Jack Dempsey.

Do not keep it with crayfish or crabs, which destroy plants, eat them and uproot everything in the tank. Floating plants are the better choice with them.

Choose companion plants that will not completely overshadow it.

Cryptocoryne parva from Sri Lanka is the smallest of all Cryptocorynes (only 3-6 cm tall and a rosette less than 5-8 cm wide). It is one of the few species that does not significantly change its leaf shape and colour depending on cultivation conditions. It needs more light than most other Cryptocorynes because it almost loses its leaf plate under water. So, it must never be overshadowed by other plants. Very recommendable foreground plant.

Cryptocoryne parva is the smallest species of all known crypts. Its leaves are narrow and oval, often less than 5 cm (2 inches) long, and green. It forms a small bush of many lanceolate, elongated green leaves gathered in a wide rosette. The leaves are vibrant dark green, flat and elongated, without frilling. Typical height is 3 – 8 cm (~1 – 3 inches).

It is one of the few Cryptocoryne species whose leaf colour, shape and form do not change significantly when the environment changes. Because of its small size it is ideal as a ground cover in the foreground, especially in small tanks and nano aquariums.

The first Cryptocoryne species was described in 1779 as Arum spirale by Anders Jahan Retzius. Later the plant entered the hobby and was sold under different names. In 1970 Hendrik Cornelis Dirk recognized it as a separate species.

Benefits

  • Aquascape: one of the best choices for aquascapes, particularly Iwagumi.
  • Prevents gas pockets: the root system helps break up anaerobic pockets in the substrate. Hydrogen sulfide pockets (H2S, smells like rotten eggs) can be very dangerous to fish and shrimp.
  • Foraging place: an additional place for biofilm to grow, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Shelter: provides hiding spots for shy fish and shrimp.
  • Oxygenation: like all plants, it helps oxygenate the water.

Buying

Numerous Cryptocoryne varieties exist, so check the label to be sure it is Cryptocoryne parva. A potted plant sells for a few dollars, and the quantity needed depends on tank size. Choose plants with lush green leaves, abundant roots and no cuts or holes in the leaves.

Quarantine

Unless the plant is certainly safe, for example grown in vitro in an undamaged, unopened pot, quarantine it before putting it into the aquarium.

  • The plant can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.).
  • It could also have been treated with chemicals (pesticides) against parasites, snails, etc. These chemicals are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Other crypts

  • Cryptocoryne wendtii: the most variable crypt, with forms differing in colour and leaf shape; its appearance may change significantly with tank conditions. The most common are 'wendtii green' (oblong dark green leaves) and 'wendtii red' (elongated reddish-brown leaves). It grows to 15+ cm and tolerates low to high light.
  • Cryptocoryne undulata: from Sri Lanka, grows in fast-flowing streams and rivers. It has a small internode between the leaves. Undemanding, adaptable, grows up to 25 cm.
  • Cryptocoryne crispatula: tall, 50+ cm, with long leaf blades with corrugated edges, lush green to bronze. Suited to large tanks, placed in the back; needs a lot of light and good fertilization.
  • Cryptocoryne spiralis: grows on the coastal lands of rivers and streams in India and Bangladesh. Long, slender leaves with slightly wavy edges, bright green to brown. Emersed it reaches about 15 cm, submersed about 30 cm. Medium growth rate, needs a lot of light.
  • Cryptocoryne lucens: smaller and plainer, about 10 – 12 cm high, suitable for foreground or midground. Forms thick vegetation with bright green flat leaves, grows slowly and has almost the same requirements as Cryptocoryne parva.
